topic: Silence after the price: closer states the price, customer squirms, closer stays silent, customer says yes. Lesson: whoever speaks first after the price loses.
'I need to think about it' -> 'Totally fair. What exactly do you need to think about?' -> real objection (money) appears.
Selling is helping: if you believe your product helps, NOT selling it is the selfish move.
Status: the person who needs the deal more loses. Act like the expert, not the beggar.
'I need to talk to my wife/partner' -> 'If they agreed, is there anything else stopping you?' -> collect all objections first.
'Just tell me the price' mid-pitch -> 'I want the core ideas to be clear first. Two more minutes.' Price comes after they agree with the plan.
Tonality: certainty in your voice sells more than the words. Statements down, not up like questions.
Volume makes you good: 100 conversations teach you more than 10 courses. Reps beat theory.
Cold lead gives one-word answers -> pattern break: 'I notice short answers. I called to see if I can help. Is now a bad time?'
Prospect talks for minutes about their holiday -> closer stays warm, then steers back with a question. Avoid the friend zone.
Three levels of pain: surface problem, business impact, personal impact. People buy at level three.
Ask where they want to be, not just what's wrong. The gap between now and goal is what they pay for.
'Maybe in 3-4 months' -> closer doesn't pitch, explains why it makes no sense to continue today; customer: 'Actually... could we start now?'
Customer asks for 4 instalments -> closer agrees only in return for a case study and 2 referrals. Give and take.
Mental trap: you project YOUR budget onto the customer. 'That's expensive' is often your thought, not theirs.
Blockers: ask what stopped them from solving this before. That answer is your future objection, handle it early.
No objections left but no decision -> pattern interrupt: 'I'm starting to doubt this is right for you. Did I misunderstand something?'
'Send me more info by email' -> 'Happy to. What specifically do you want to see, so I send the right thing?' -> real question appears.
The 7-hour rule: people buy after roughly 7 hours of contact with you. Content builds those hours for you.
No-shows: a short reminder the day before and a reason to show up cuts no-shows. Never chase with guilt.
Customer: 'Why can't I just do it myself?' -> closer explains options (alone, DIY tools, with help) and lets the customer choose the vehicle.
Qualifying: closer asks 'If we find the right solution today, are you in a position to start?' before pitching anything.
Create status: be a little hard to get. Set the agenda of the call yourself in the first 30 seconds.
After the yes: stop selling. Take payment calmly, explain next steps. Talking more after yes creates doubt.
Customer: 'Can you do a discount?' -> closer: 'What would a discount change for you?' -> it's not about price.
End of first call: closer books the meeting only if there's a real problem; disqualifies a tire-kicker politely.
Your energy is the first thing they buy. Stand up, smile, prepare before every call.
A script is not a cage: it's a map. Pros use a structure so they can listen instead of thinking what to say.
'I've been burned before by courses/agencies' -> closer acknowledges, asks what went wrong, shows how this is different with proof.
Down-sell: customer can't afford the full offer -> closer offers a smaller first step instead of a discount.
Stop convincing, start diagnosing: doctors don't beg patients to take medicine.
Ask 'What happens if nothing changes in the next 6 months?' Then stay quiet.
Customer doubts it works for them -> closer shows proof from someone in the same situation, not generic testimonials.
Closer sets the frame: 'Here's how the next 30 minutes go: I ask questions, if it fits I show you, if not I tell you. Fair?'
Track 3 numbers daily: conversations, offers made, yeses. What you measure improves.
Slow down when you say the price. Fast talk sounds nervous; slow sounds certain.
'It's not the right time' -> 'When would be the right time, and what would be different then?'
Big promise: closer summarises the customer's goal in their own words before showing the plan; customer: 'Exactly.'
Fear of rejection: a 'no' is information, not an insult. Ask what made it a no.
People buy the result, not the product: sell the after-picture.
